ONE ROW DIFFERS FROM THE ROUND DIRECTION'S ARITHMETIC, AND IT HAS TO. `fixes-for-the-identity-test.md` says "seventeen rows carry `red: false` ... and check 18 carries `red: true`". Check 1 is recorded `red: true` instead, because check 1 is "`make build && make test` green, and `bun test` green, from the repository root" and `bun test` exits 1 on this tree — made red by the very check-18 test this round was told to write. The same file says "The only failure in it may be the new check-18 test", so the direction and the fact agree about what the tree does; only the count of red rows differs. Decision `passing-row-reason` says "Any acceptance check that passes today is recorded as passing", and `green-criterion` refuses "a `red: false` row with no reason"; a `red: false` row for check 1 would have to claim `bun test` is green, which would be a false reason. So the record is sixteen passing rows and two red ones — 18, and 1 because of 18. `make build && make test` on its own is exit 0 (834 .NET tests, 619 + 56 + 11 + 148, all passed).

WHAT THIS ROUND TOUCHED. `ts/metalang/app.test.tsx` only: `git status --short` is `M ts/metalang/app.test.tsx` and `git diff --stat` is 73 insertions, 0 deletions — one new `describe` of three tests appended between the two existing identity describes. No existing test was rewritten, re-pointed, weakened or deleted; `ts/metalang/guardrails.test.ts` and everything under `.agents/` are untouched, as the direction requires. No production file, dependency, interface or skeleton signature was changed.

THE FIXTURE PINS THE DECISION, NOT JUST THE CHECK'S EXAMPLE. Decision `member-identity-unique` says the place "counts among the rows sharing the name rather than among all of the declaration's members, so adding an unrelated member above them leaves both identities as they were". So the fixture declares `Name` first and then the two `PrecheckAsync` members: counting among the rows sharing the name gives `PrecheckAsync#1` and `PrecheckAsync#2`, while counting among all of the declaration's members would give `#2` and `#3`. A fixture of the two overloads alone would pass under either rule and prove the weaker one.

THE THIRD CASE PASSES, WHICH IS WHAT CHECK 18 ASKS OF IT. "A declaration with no repeated name is drawn exactly as before" cannot fail today — it guards the behaviour that keeps every target written against the kit working — so that test is GREEN now and the other two are RED. The row is still `red: true` with an empty reason, because the check as a whole fails: coverage rows are per acceptance check, and two of this check's three cases fail. All three cases are named in the pasted output, which the criterion requires.

A SINGLE-FILE `bun test <file>` EXITS 1 EVEN WITH EVERY TEST PASSING. `bunfig.toml` sets `coverageThreshold = 0.75` across the whole tree, so `bun test ts/metalang/kit.test.ts` reports 28 pass / 0 fail and still exits 1 on the floor, as does `bun test ts/metalang/render.test.ts` at 38 pass / 0 fail. That is pre-existing and not caused by this round; the per-check evidence in the rows above is the named tests passing, and the full-suite `bun test` is what check 11 reads the floor off.

NOTHING WAS ESCALATED. The three tests needed no seam the skeleton does not expose: they drive the real `Page` component through the existing `pageFor`/`matched` helpers and read the page with jsdom, exactly as checks 2 to 5 already do, which is where the direction said to write them.

WHERE THE IMPLEMENT WORKER HAS TO LOOK. `ts/metalang/app.tsx:747-760` — `identityOf` returns the member's own name with nothing making it unique, so both rows carry `PrecheckAsync` today. The decision's wording is the spec: a name occurring once among its declaration's members stays exactly as it is, a name occurring more than once gives each of those rows that name, a number sign and its place among the rows sharing that name counting from one in source order, and no row carries the shared name on its own.

The only record behind it is his refusal of all offered options plus a blanket "FIX IT CORRECTLY now", which rails-decisions says "approves only items already individually approved — never a new one."

I do not approve 120 I do not approve a dely I do not APPROVE a hack.  FIX IT CORRECTLY now."}` at 2026-11-13T22:24:48-06:00. The options that package offered were accept-the-ambiguity, ban the repeat in the language, and issue 120 / delay (.dev/inprocess/114-kit-page-narration/three-choices-nobody-made.md), so no spelling was ever put to him. I scanned every decisions.json under .../jarvis/data/packages for a later approval of an identity format and found none; the last records of this run are passing-row-reason (22:12) and fix-round-authority (22:35), neither about the format.

The contract records the whole mechanism as decided: contract.md:29 `member-identity-unique` — "an identity written as that name, a number sign, and the row's place among the members of that declaration carrying that same name, counting from one in the order the source declares them — `PrecheckAsync#1` and `PrecheckAsync#2`" — and its provenance sentence says only "Tim ordered this ... answering `overload-target` with none of the choices offered and the instruction to fix it correctly now." Every other decision in that section reads "Tim approved this as written on <date> ... the record is `results/decisions.json` in <package>" (contract.md:13, :15, :33); this is the one decision with no approval claim and no record path.

The gap was known and closed by self-decision, not by a yes: commit 3e71f8c ("Decide how the repeated-member identity is spelled") states "The architecture round's lie-catcher found the decision named the two parts and not the spelling, which is the published selector format, so it would have been defaulted by whoever wrote the test or the code", and the fix was to write the spelling into contract.md and acceptance check 18. .dev/inprocess/114-kit-page-narration/three-choices-nobody-made.md already classified it: "the fix changes the published identity format".

This round encodes it: ts/metalang/app.test.tsx:1925 and :1928 assert the exact strings `PrecheckAsync#1` / `PrecheckAsync#2`; :1935 asserts the bare shared name reaches no row; :1904-1910 orders the fixture `Name`, `PrecheckAsync`, `PrecheckAsync` specifically to pin the counting basis (the TDD notes: "A fixture of the two overloads alone would pass under either rule and prove the weaker one"); :1952 asserts no `#` on an unrepeated declaration. The result's own notes then hand the unapproved wording to the next stage as law: "The decision's wording is the spec."

What remains unproven: no record anywhere of Tim's explicit yes to the `#`-plus-ordinal spelling, or to numbering among the shared rows rather than among all members — the two parts of the format that JARVIS beats and every target written against the released kit will depend on.

refutationAttempts: Tried to find an approval for the `#`-plus-ordinal spelling: read the `overload-target` record itself, then scanned every package decisions.json in the JARVIS package store, then grepped the run folder and `.agents/` for `overload-target`. The only record is "answer": "none" with the note "FIX IT CORRECTLY now" — no option naming any format, and no later record approving one.

Tried the reading that "FIX IT CORRECTLY now" authorizes the format as implementation detail: rails-decisions:24 asks whether the choice outlives its function and makes other code depend on it. `data-member="PrecheckAsync#1"` is the string JARVIS beats and every target written against the released kit must use; the project's own prior rulings call it "the published selector format" (commit 3e71f8c) and "the published identity format" (three-choices-nobody-made.md). It is Tim's, not the agent's.

Tried treating the contract itself as the authorization, since "Scope changes ONLY by the human editing the contract": commit 3e71f8c is co-authored by Claude and its own message says the spelling "would have been defaulted by whoever wrote the test or the code", and the decision's provenance sentence claims only that Tim "ordered this", never that he approved this wording — while all thirteen sibling decisions name a package and say "approved this as written". rails-decisions:30 forbids anchoring approval to what is already in the tree.

Tried whether a prior adversary round already settled it, to avoid re-opening a ruling: the architecture round's lie-catcher raised exactly this gap and it was closed by the agent writing the spelling into the contract rather than by a yes, so the finding was closed without the approval — not settled.
